content: The almond, scientifically known as Prunus dulcis (synonym Amygdalus dulcis Mill.), is a species of the genus Prunus within the subfamily Prunoideae of the family Rosaceae. Within the genus Prunus, it is classified alongside the peach in the subgenus Amygdalus, which is distinguished by its corrugated seed shell. The almond is also the seed of this tree. The almond tree is native to Southwest Asia, spanning regions from northwestern Saudi Arabia, through western Jordan, Israel, Lebanon, western Syria, and into southern Turkey. It is a small deciduous tree that grows to a height of 4–10 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 30 cm. Young shoots are initially green, turning purplish when exposed to sunlight, and eventually becoming gray in their second year. The flowers of the almond tree are white or pale pink, measuring 3–5 cm in diameter, with five petals. They appear singly or in pairs before the leaves emerge in early spring. The fruit is 5–6 cm long, with a downy outer coat. Unlike other members of the genus Prunus, such as plums and cherries, the outer covering (exocarp) of the almond is reduced to a leathery gray-green hull. Inside the hull is a hard shell that encases the edible kernel, commonly referred to as a nut in culinary terms, though botanically it is not a true nut. Typically, one kernel is present, though occasionally two may be found. The hard, stony shell is botanically termed the endocarp. The almond matures in autumn, approximately 7–8 months after flowering. The wild form of the domesticated almond grows in parts of the Levant, where it was likely first cultivated. Wild almonds contain the glycoside amygdalin, which, when crushed, chewed, or otherwise injured, transforms into toxic prussic acid (hydrogen cyanide). Before domestication, wild almonds were likely processed through leaching or roasting to remove their toxicity. Domesticated almonds, however, are non-toxic due to a genetic mutation that eliminates amygdalin. This mutation was likely propagated by early farmers, initially unintentionally and later intentionally in orchards. Almonds are believed to be among the earliest domesticated fruit trees, as they can be grown from seed without requiring propagation through suckers or cuttings. Domesticated almonds appear in the archaeological record as early as the Early Bronze Age (3000–2000 BCE) in the Near East. A notable example is the almonds found in Tutankhamun's tomb in Egypt (circa 1325 BCE), likely imported from the Levant. Almonds are called Lawz in Arabic, Baadaam in Persian, Urdu, and Hindi. Major almond producers include Greece, Iran, Italy, Morocco, Portugal, Spain, Syria, Turkey, and the United States, with California being the largest producer globally. In California, almonds are the sixth leading agricultural product and the top agricultural export. However, due to cases of salmonella traced to almonds in 2001 and 2004, regulations were introduced in 2007 requiring raw almonds to be steam-pasteurized or chemically treated with propylene oxide before being sold in the United States. The pollination of California's almond orchards represents the largest annual managed pollination event in the world, involving nearly one million beehives, which account for almost half of all beehives in the United States. Pollination is managed by brokers who contract with migratory beekeepers from at least 38 states. There are two forms of almond plants: one producing sweet almonds (often with white flowers) and the other producing bitter almonds (often with pink flowers). Sweet almonds contain a fixed oil and are used in culinary and medicinal applications. Bitter almonds, which are broader and shorter than sweet almonds, contain about 50% of the fixed oil found in sweet almonds, as well as the enzyme emulsin. In the presence of water, emulsin acts on the glycoside amygdalin, yielding glucose, cyanide, and benzaldehyde (the essential oil of bitter almonds). Bitter almonds can yield 6–8% hydrogen cyanide and must have the cyanide removed before consumption. Historically, bitter almond extract was used medicinally, but its effects are severe even in small doses and can be fatal in larger doses. Almonds have also been used as a preventative for alcohol intoxication, and folklore claims they are poisonous to foxes. Culinary uses of almonds are diverse. They are often eaten raw or toasted and are used in dishes such as baklava and nougat. Almond butter, a spread similar to peanut butter, is popular among those with peanut allergies and for its less salty taste. Green almonds, the young, developing fruit of the almond tree, can be eaten whole when the outer shell is still soft and fleshy. These are available from mid-April to mid-June and are sometimes pickled or brined to extend their shelf life. Almond flour, made from sweet almonds, is low in carbohydrates and suitable for low-carb diets or for individuals with diabetes. A standard serving of almond flour (1 cup) contains 20 grams of carbohydrates, 10 grams of which are dietary fiber, resulting in a net carbohydrate content of 10 grams per cup. Almond flour is thus desirable for baking cakes and bread in carbohydrate-restricted diets. In Greece, ground blanched almonds are used as the base for a variety of desserts called amygdalota, which are traditionally served at weddings due to their white color. Almonds can also be processed into almond milk, a dairy substitute suitable for lactose-intolerant individuals and vegans. Sweet almonds are used in marzipan, nougat, macaroons, and other desserts. Almonds are a rich source of vitamin E, containing 24 mg per 100 g, and are high in monounsaturated fats, which help lower LDL cholesterol. The Marcona almond variety, originating in Spain, is shorter, rounder, sweeter, and more delicate in texture than other varieties. It is traditionally served lightly fried in oil and is used in Spanish desserts such as turrón. Almond oil, known as Oleum Amygdalae, is prepared from either sweet or bitter almonds. It is a glycerol oleate with a slight odor and nutty taste, almost insoluble in alcohol but soluble in chloroform or ether. Sweet almond oil, extracted from the dried kernel, is traditionally used by massage therapists as an effective emollient. Historically, almond syrup was an emulsion of sweet and bitter almonds, often made with barley syrup or orange-flower water and sugar. Almonds are associated with various health benefits. Edgar Cayce, regarded as the father of American holistic medicine, recommended including almonds in the diet for improved complexion, enhanced digestion, and cancer prevention. Recent research links almond consumption to increased levels of high-density lipoproteins (HDL) and reduced levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL). In Ayurveda, almonds are considered a brain and nervous system tonic, promoting intellectual development and longevity. Almond oil, known as Roghan Badam in Ayurveda and Unani medicine, is considered a nutritive aphrodisiac and is used for both massage and internal consumption. Recent studies have demonstrated that almond constituents have anti-inflammatory, immunity-boosting, and anti-hepatotoxic effects. Culturally, almonds hold significant importance. In Israel, the almond tree is one of the first to flower, symbolizing vigilance and promise. In the Bible, almonds are mentioned ten times, often symbolizing God's rapid judgment or divine favor. Almond branches are also used in Christian symbolism, representing the Virgin Birth of Jesus. In India, almonds are believed to enhance brain function, while in Chinese culture, they symbolize enduring sadness and feminine beauty. The word almond derives from Old French almande or alemande, which traces back to the Greek amygdala. The prefix almay have been influenced by the Arabic article al.
